extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of paleontology, evolutionary biology, and history/philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating paleontological theories and models (especially of extinction) for their explanatory power, empirical fit to the fossil record, level of abstraction, and contributions to disciplinary autonomy. Includes guidance on what makes a fruitful/modeling strategy in paleobiology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model simplicity, parsimony, and intuitiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor models that are simple, have relatively few and well-understood parameters, and are biologically intuitive (Gould’s advocacy of the power function was because it was simple, general, and deeply intuitive on a biological level).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity aids understanding and explanation, and makes models more extendable across taxa and stratigraphic ranges; prefer models that trade off some quantitative accuracy for conceptual clarity and fewer parameters when that yields broader insight or applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom from excessive phenotypic detail / appropriate level of abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Models that are relatively free from the phenotypic detail of specific taxa (e.g., the species-as-particles approach) can reveal general laws and produce null expectations about broad patterns of extinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use higher-level abstractions when the goal is to test whether macro-patterns arise from taxon- specific mechanisms or from generic processes; be explicit about what is being ignored and why (and check limits of the abstraction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory breadth and generativity (fruitfulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good paleontological model/theory can disclose laws of nature and have a prodigious range of applicability; it should suggest new kinds of fossil trends and new empirical questions to pursue (Gould: fruitful lawmaking strategy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess models not only for fit but for their ability to generate new predictions, suggest new empirical searches (e.g., for certain fossil trends), and provide conceptual tools that can be used across multiple cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit to empirical fossil-record patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Models should account for major features of the fossil record (e.g., absence of clear evidence of progress, patterns of taxonomic and morphological rates, rarity of transitional forms, abrupt disappearances vs gradual loss).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a model reproduces observed macroevolutionary patterns (diversity trajectories, stasis, abrupt turnover, stratigraphic distributions) and whether mismatches reflect model failure or artifact of preservation/sampling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing selective versus nonselective extinction (null model testing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly test whether extinction proneness is an inherent property of taxa (selective) or whether extinctions can be modeled as chance events in a 'field of bullets' (nonselective/null models as advocated by Raup).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate and compare null (nonselective) models to selective hypotheses; use simulations and statistical tests to assess whether observed patterns require taxon-specific vulnerabilities or can arise by chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple lines of evidence for causal inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Causal claims about extinction (e.g., bolide impact at K–Pg) should be supported by convergent stratigraphic/geochemical and global-pattern evidence (the iridium anomaly at the K–Pg boundary as an example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require geochemical, stratigraphic, paleontological, and biogeographic congruence before inferring catastrophic versus gradual causes; evaluate temporal coincidence and mechanism plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical distinctiveness from population genetics / theoretical independence
rubrics_metrics.description: To justify paleontology’s theoretical independence, the phenomena it studies (e.g., mass extinction regularities) should not be predictable or explainable by population genetics alone and should provide special insight into evolutionary processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the target phenomena require paleontological concepts/tools (e.g., stratigraphic context, macroevolutionary aggregates) beyond microevolutionary explanations; demonstrate phenomena that are irreducible to population-genetic accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for disciplinary autonomy (intrinsicality, transmission, continuity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three conditions for a discipline’s emergence as autonomous: (1) Intrinsicality — the subject (e.g., extinction) must be a real phenomenon of general evolutionary significance; (2) Transmission — the theoretical problems and unique tools must be passed from veteran to apprentice practitioners; (3) Continuity — magnitudes of differences between versions of a practice should track magnitudes of differences in fitness (smaller practice differences → smaller fitness contributions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing for a discipline’s autonomy, document the unique subject-matter significance, the inheritance of specialized methods/practices across generations, and show that practical variations have fitness-relevant consequences that map continuously onto outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rarity-as-precursor and causal linkage reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical reasoning that 'rarity precedes extinction'—use observed rarity and inferred 'injurious agencies' to explain eventual extinction (Darwin’s methodological point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use population size and rarity trends as diagnostic signals, but distinguish rarity caused by long-term decline from sampling artifacts; link rarity to plausible causal processes (competition, environmental change) rather than treating rarity as explanans without mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for testable and irreducible theoretical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Paleontology should generate testable, irreducible theories about historical pattern (Gould: 'generators of testable and irreducible theories about pattern in the history of life').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor hypotheses that make clear empirical predictions in the fossil record and that cannot be straightforwardly reduced to other disciplinary frameworks; emphasize empirical testability and irreducibility when proposing theoretical contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for apparent suddenness via temporal resolution considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent rapid extinctions in the stratigraphic column may reflect coarse temporal resolution; models/explanations must account for intervals between formations and possibility of slow extermination masked by sampling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before inferring sudden catastrophe, evaluate stratigraphic resolution, sampling gaps, and immigration/competitive replacement scenarios that can produce apparently abrupt patterns; use high-resolution stratigraphy where possible.
